candidates.attacker_control: Untrusted Groovy source compiled with SandboxTransformer (the library's stated purpose: 'Executes untrusted Groovy script safely'). The attacker chooses the receiver expression of a method-pointer/lambda expression, e.g. `"cmd".execute().&toString` or `new File("/etc/passwd").&text`, so the nested call is attacker-authored and evaluates at pointer-creation time.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that most other branches do re-transform children (CastExpression line 599; transformArguments lines 290-303; transformObjectExpression; AttributeExpression/PropertyExpression read paths), which shows the intended invariant and makes this branch an outlier rather than deliberate. Checked that the framework default path (super.transform(exp) -> exp.transformExpression(this)) is the only thing that would transform children of an unmatched node, and it is not reached for matched MethodPointerExpression. Checked that if children were pre-transformed bottom-up by the framework, the explicit transform(...) calls used elsewhere in the same class would double-wrap already-generated Checker.checked* calls and break the library, indicating traversal is top-down and omitted children truly remain raw. Checked SandboxedMethodClosure.doCall overloads: they check invocation of the pointer, so the residual issue is specifically pointer-creation-time evaluation. Not verified: behavior under Groovy 2.4.7 by compilation/execution.
candidates.impact: Sandbox policy bypass / sandbox escape: operations the host's interceptor intends to forbid (process execution, file access, reflection, etc.) are performed unchecked, contradicting the library's guarantee that every such operation is routed through Checker for interception; later invocation checks do not undo the side effect.
candidates.prerequisites: Host compiles the script with SandboxTransformer and registers a GroovyInterceptor (e.g. whitelist/deny-all value filter) intended to mediate every external interaction; the attacker's nested operation in the receiver position is denied by that interceptor if it were intercepted.
candidates.root_cause: In SandboxTransformer.VisitorImpl.innerTransform (src/main/java/org/kohsuke/groovy/sandbox/SandboxTransformer.java:394-400), a MethodPointerExpression is rewritten to `new SandboxedMethodClosure(mpe.getExpression(), mpe.getMethodName())` using the original, untransformed child expressions. Unlike the other branches (e.g. CastExpression line 599, PropertyExpression lines 429/432, AttributeExpression 419/422, constructor/static-call arguments via transformArguments lines 290-304), the receiver sub-expression is never run through transform(). Because VisitorImpl.transform() returns the replacement node as soon as innerTransform matches (lines 311-318) and never lets the framework's default `super.transform(exp)`/exp.transformExpression(this) path process this node's children, any method call, property read, or constructor call embedded in the receiver expression is emitted into the transformed class as a plain call with no Checker.checked* wrapper. (The same omission pattern also exists for the dynamic method-name expression `arg1 = call.getMethod()` at line 360; treated here as the same root cause, not a second candidate.)
candidates.title: Method-pointer receiver expression is copied into the rewritten AST without transform(), leaving nested calls un-instrumented (sandbox interception bypass)
candidates.trace: Script text -> parser produces MethodPointerExpression(expression = MethodCallExpression(`"cmd".execute()`), methodName = `toString`) -> SandboxTransformer.call() -> VisitorImpl.transform(exp) -> innerTransform matches the `exp instanceof MethodPointerExpression` branch (line 394) -> replacement ConstructorCallExpression contains the raw receiver child -> transform() returns immediately (lines 311-318), so neither the raw child nor the replacement is visited again -> codegen emits a direct `String.execute()` call with no Checker.checkedCall wrapper -> GroovyInterceptor.onMethodCall is never consulted for that call -> command/file/reflection side effect happens inside the host JVM. Invoking the resulting SandboxedMethodClosure later is checked (SandboxedMethodClosure.doCall -> Checker.checkedCall), but that is too late: the un-instrumented receiver call has already executed.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no Groovy compiler/interceptor run was performed; Groovy 2.4.7 traversal semantics (ClassCodeExpressionTransformer/Expression.transformExpression) were reasoned from this repository's source structure, since the Groovy framework sources are outside the snapshot. It is not confirmed that a real script such as `"cmd".execute().&toString` compiles to the AST shape assumed, nor whether upstream later wrapped this child in transform() (external comparison was out of scope), so this remains a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-693 Protection Mechanism Failure / sandbox escape via incomplete AST instrumentation

coverage_summary: Snapshot contains 22 files (all main sources plus pom/README/site docs); there is no src/test tree, so no tests could corroborate expected behavior. I read every main source file in full (SandboxTransformer, ScopeTrackingClassCodeExpressionTransformer, Checker, GroovyInterceptor, GroovyValueFilter, ClosureSupport, InvokerChain family, Ops, Super, SandboxedMethodClosure, StackVariableSet) and the build/site files. P1 relation scope reports 22/22 files indexed, 194 symbols, 744 call rows, 419 edges, no file hash mismatches, and explicitly no SAST/oracle findings or runtime reachability analysis; the only navigation fact was pom.xml as a configuration file. No builds, tests, scans, or code execution were performed, and no external/upstream diff, CVE, or patch data was consulted.
limitations: No execution or compilation was possible: all conclusions are static, and the Groovy 2.4.x AST traversal semantics (ClassCodeExpressionTransformer.transform / Expression.transformExpression) are outside the snapshot and were inferred from how this code must behave to avoid double-wrapping its own Checker.checked* output.

The snapshot has no tests and no upstream history/patches, so intended-versus-injected changes could not be diffed; the candidate may correspond to a long-standing upstream limitation rather than the case's specific defect.
The P1 index is navigational only (no data flow, reachability, or taint proof), and it exposed no security findings to corroborate or refute the candidate.

Scope-tracking, exception/control-flow, and Closure delegation paths were reviewed by reading only; no dynamic confirmation of exact runtime dispatch (e.g. which doCall overload Groovy 2.4.7 selects) was obtained.

rejected_leads.lead: Variable-scope over-approximation in ScopeTrackingClassCodeExpressionTransformer (visitIfElse/visitBlockStatement share one StackVariableSet per construct, lines 68-123): a name declared in one branch can be treated as a local variable while visiting another branch.
rejected_leads.reason: I could not demonstrate an unchecked evaluation: method calls and property reads/writes on such a name are still wrapped in Checker.checked* with the actual runtime receiver value, so interceptors still see the operation; only bare identifier reads would skip a property-get check, which was not shown to reach a forbidden value. Upstream-looking design, no concrete bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: FieldExpression left-hand sides of assignments are not intercepted (SandboxTransformer.java:512-516).
rejected_leads.reason: Documented in-code limitation; the expression only concerns fields of the class being transformed (script/this-local state), and no source evidence showed attacker-reachable cross-object field access through it.

rejected_leads.lead: Checker.checkedComparison bypasses interceptors when lhs is null (Checker.java:514-518).
rejected_leads.reason: The shortcut only performs static ScriptBytecodeAdapter dispatch on a null operand; no user-controlled method is invoked at that point, and the comment states the rationale. No concrete interceptor bypass demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: checkedCast deliberately ignores return values and invokes every interface method with default arguments (Checker.java:539-606).
rejected_leads.reason: These invocations are deliberately routed through the interceptor chain (onMethodCall/onStaticCall/onNewInstance), so interception still occurs; no missing check found in the source.

rejected_leads.lead: Incomplete interception of Closure built-in properties and Closure delegation (ClosureSupport/Checker.java:246-293, BUILTIN_PROPERTIES list including thisObject/metaClass).
rejected_leads.reason: BUILTIN_PROPERTIES only skips delegation of the access to owner/delegate; the access is still delivered to onGetProperty with the closure receiver, and sandboxing of Closure methods is explicitly the interceptor's responsibility. No attacker-controlled bypass was established from the source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: SandboxedMethodClosure single-argument invocation bypass (historically caused by missing doCall(Object) override).
rejected_leads.reason: The snapshot already overrides doCall(Object[]) , doCall() and doCall(Object) (all routed to Checker.checkedCall), so the classic single-arg bypass appears covered; any residual concern is about the pointer receiver evaluation, which is the submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Untransformed dynamic method-name expression (`arg1 = call.getMethod()`, SandboxTransformer.java:360).
rejected_leads.reason: Same root-cause pattern as the submitted candidate (a child copied into a replacement node without transform()); not listed as a separate candidate per the one-candidate rule.

summary: Reviewed the full 22-file snapshot of groovy-sandbox 1.20-SNAPSHOT (compile-time Groovy sandbox: SandboxTransformer rewrites untrusted script AST so every external interaction routes through Checker/GroovyInterceptor). All main sources were read; no tests are present in the snapshot. The strongest source-evidence lead is an instrumentation gap in VisitorImpl.innerTransform: the MethodPointerExpression branch builds the replacement SandboxedMethodClosure node from the raw receiver expression without recursively calling transform(), so nested calls inside a method-pointer receiver are emitted un-wrapped and never reach any registered interceptor. One candidate is submitted; several other observed weaknesses were considered but rejected as unconfirmed or by-design.
